blocks.title: Basic terms
rows: A formal language used to write instructions that a computer can carry out.
An organised set (sequence) of instructions written for one particular task.
A finite sequence of clear, ordered steps that solves a problem.
The grammatical rules for writing valid instructions in a language.
Writing the solution as instructions in a programming language.
A visual picture of an algorithm or program logic, drawn with standard shapes and arrows.
A fault in a program that can give wrong results or unexpected behaviour.
Finding, investigating and fixing the faults (bugs) in a program.

blocks.title: Three kinds of code
rows: Human-readable instructions written by the programmer (for example a .py file).
Output of a compiler or assembler; it commonly holds machine instructions plus linking information and may still need linking (for example .obj).
Binary-encoded instructions (0s and 1s) that the processor executes directly.

blocks.title: One-line memory aid
blocks.text: Algorithm = ordered solution. Flowchart = visual logic. Coding = writing instructions. Debugging = correcting faults.

**Low-level languages** (machine language and assembly language) closely mirror what the processor does, so they are generally **architecture-dependent**. **High-level languages** use readable instructions and abstractions. Languages are also grouped into five generations (1GL to 5GL); a higher number means a higher level of abstraction.

blocks.title: Five generations of languages
rows: Binary instructions using 0s and 1s; directly executable by the relevant processor
Uses mnemonics; an assembler converts it into machine code
C, C++, Java, BASIC, Visual Basic, Python, JavaScript
Commonly linked with databases, reporting and numerical work
Describe relationships, rules or constraints rather than step-by-step procedures

blocks.title: Important distinctions
items: **Python, Perl and Ruby** are high-level scripting languages and are generally classified as 3GLs. Scripting does not automatically mean 4GL.
**Lisp and OPS5** are important AI languages, but not every AI language is a 5GL.
Assembly is the usual exam answer for the **second generation of computers**, although machine code and early high-level languages existed then too.
Hardware generations and language generations are two different classifications.

blocks.title: Language processors
rows: Translates assembly instructions into machine-code object files.
Translates source code into another form such as object code, machine code or bytecode.
Executes instructions through an interpreting environment.
Combines object files and libraries to create an executable (or other linked output).

blocks.title: Exam comparison
rows: Translates the program as a whole, then gives object code as output
Processes and executes instructions step by step
Converts assembly language to machine code

blocks.title: Real systems are messier
blocks.text: Real implementations may mix compilation and interpretation. Not every compiler produces native machine code (some give bytecode), and not every interpreter works one source line at a time. For basic exams stay with the conventional picture above.

blocks.title: Software category
items: Translators (assembler, compiler, interpreter) are classified as **system software**.
Application software such as a word processor is **not** a language-processor category.
Compiler input is **source code**; its conventional output is **object code**.

rows: Machine code runs directly on the processor, so machine language is the expected basic-exam answer for direct execution.
Actual speed depends on the algorithm, generated instructions, optimisation and hardware. Handwritten machine code is not automatically fastest.
High-level languages generally give greater source-code portability, but you still need a suitable compiler or interpreter, compatible libraries and operating-system support.
Easier reading, coding, debugging and maintenance; quicker development; greater source-code portability.
Some implementations add runtime or memory overhead. Lower efficiency is the usual stated limitation of high-level languages, but it is a possible limitation, not a universal rule.

blocks.text: Machine language and assembly language are both low-level. Machine language is the one the CPU executes directly; assembly needs an assembler first.

blocks.title: From 1843 to 1972
items: Ada Lovelace published notes on Charles Babbage's proposed Analytical Engine that included an algorithm for Bernoulli numbers.
FORTRAN (Formula Translation) was developed by an IBM team led by John Backus; its first compiler came out in 1957 and a manual appeared in 1956.
ALGOL (Algorithmic Language) began as an influential language family.
LISP (List Processing) was created by John McCarthy for list processing, symbolic computation and AI; an influential paper followed in 1960.
COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language) was designed for commercial data processing such as banking, payroll, billing and insurance.
BASIC (Beginner's All-purpose Symbolic Instruction Code) was developed by John Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz.
Simula 67 by Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard, widely recognised as the first object-oriented programming language.
Pascal was developed by Niklaus Wirth.
Around 1972
Dennis Ritchie developed C at Bell Labs during the early Unix era.
Prolog came from Alain Colmerauer's team, particularly Philippe Roussel, with important contributions from Robert Kowalski; used for logic programming.

blocks.title: FORTRAN dates and title
blocks.text: FORTRAN: manual in 1956, first compiler in 1957. It is more precisely called the first widely adopted high-level language, and it is linked with scientific and numerical computing.

blocks.title: From the 1970s to 2014
items: Smalltalk: Alan Kay and colleagues at Xerox PARC advanced object-oriented programming.
Bjarne Stroustrup began C with Classes at Bell Labs in 1979; the name C++ was adopted in 1983. It supports object-oriented and other styles.
Python: first public release, by Guido van Rossum.
Visual Basic: Microsoft's visual, event-driven development environment based on BASIC.
PHP: created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 and publicly released in 1995. It now stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor.
Java: publicly introduced by Sun Microsystems; principal designer James Gosling; early members included Mike Sheridan and Patrick Naughton; originally called Oak.
C# was announced by Microsoft.
Swift was introduced by Apple.

blocks.text: PHP did not begin in 1993; use 1994 for creation and 1995 for the public release. Java was first called Oak.

blocks.title: Essential facts about C
items: Developer: **Dennis Ritchie**, at **Bell Labs**.
Commonly cited year: **1972**.
A general-purpose, **procedural** language, closely connected with implementing Unix.
Many statements end with a **semicolon**, but not every block or construct needs one.
C is a high-level language that also has low-level facilities; 'middle-level' is only an informal textbook description.
'Mother of all languages' is just an informal nickname; FORTRAN, Lisp, ALGOL and COBOL are all older than C.
C has no built-in classes or inheritance, so it is the expected non-OOP answer among C, C++, Java and modern Visual Basic.

blocks.text: Remember by pairs: C = Ritchie, C++ = Stroustrup, Python = van Rossum, Java = Gosling, PHP = Lerdorf.

**Object-oriented programming (OOP)** organises software around objects that combine data with the operations that work on that data. For example, a Student class holds data (name, age) and operations (study, display); Alice (20) and Bob (22) are two objects made from it.

blocks.title: Class and object
rows: A definition describing the data and behaviour of a category of objects.
A particular instance of a class in class-based programming.

blocks.title: Four core concepts
rows: Groups data and operations together, with controlled access.
Exposes essential features while hiding unnecessary detail.
Lets a type or class build on another.
Supports different implementations through a shared interface.

blocks.title: Milestones and supporting languages
items: **Simula 67** is widely recognised as the first object-oriented language (Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard).
**Smalltalk** emerged in the 1970s and is commonly described as a pure object-oriented language; **Alan Kay** was a major OOP pioneer who led its development.
Languages supporting OOP: Java, Python, C++, C#, JavaScript, PHP, Ruby, Simula, Smalltalk and modern Visual Basic .NET.
**Go** has methods, interfaces and an object-oriented style, but lacks the conventional class-inheritance hierarchy of Java or C++.
No single-person founder label captures the full history of OOP.

blocks.text: Class = definition. Object = instance. Simula = early OOP. Smalltalk = pure OOP association.

rows: Hyper Text Markup Language: defines webpage structure and meaning of content. A markup language.
Cascading Style Sheets: controls colours, spacing and layout. A style-sheet language.
Adds programmable behaviour and interaction; a programming language.
Commonly used for server-side web programming.
Structured Query Language: defines, retrieves and modifies relational data.
A relational database management system (RDBMS) that uses SQL.
A JavaScript runtime, not a separate programming language.

blocks.title: Application associations
rows: Java (the usual exam answer); Kotlin is also officially supported, with a Kotlin-first approach

blocks.title: Watch the odd-one-out questions
blocks.text: Scala, Ruby, C#, C++ and Python are programming languages. Photoshop, Microsoft Word and Adobe Illustrator are application software. HTML (markup), CSS (styling) and MySQL (an RDBMS) all make a plain 'which is not a programming language' question ambiguous, and Java cannot simply be excluded from AI/ML languages.

blocks.title: Loops
rows: Repeats a block of instructions according to a condition or an iteration rule.
Often goes through a sequence or repeats a set number of times.
Repeats as long as a condition is true.
Checks the condition after the body, so the body runs at least once.

blocks.title: Development roles
rows: Studies requirements and helps design system specifications.
Designs program logic, writes, tests and maintains code.
Uses the system and gives requirements or feedback.

blocks.text: In exams, 'who designs the system' usually means the systems analyst, although developers also design the internal structure of a program.

blocks.title: Types of programming errors
rows: Violates the grammar of the language; usually detected while parsing or compiling
Malformed statement; missing required semicolon in C
Problem that occurs while the program executes (runtime = execution time)
Division by zero; Python raises ZeroDivisionError, which can be handled
Program runs but gives a wrong result because its reasoning is wrong
Not every runtime error is fatal

blocks.title: Fine points
items: Compilation errors are a broader category than syntax errors; some type errors are also caught at compile time.
Division by zero is not automatically fatal; the behaviour depends on the language and operation.
**Reserved words** have predefined meaning or restrictions in a language and are normally not available as ordinary identifiers. C examples: if, else, while, for, int, return.

blocks.text: Syntax = invalid form. Runtime = failure during execution. Logic = wrong result. Debugging = finding and fixing faults.

revision: Algorithm = finite ordered steps; flowchart = visual logic; coding = writing instructions; debugging = fixing faults.

Translators are system software; application software like Word or Photoshop is not a language processor.

LISP: John McCarthy, 1958. Pascal: Niklaus Wirth, 1970. Prolog: Colmerauer's team, 1972.
C: Dennis Ritchie, Bell Labs, around 1972. C++: Stroustrup (1979, named 1983). Python: van Rossum, 1991.
Java: James Gosling, Sun, 1995, formerly Oak. PHP: Rasmus Lerdorf, 1994/1995. C#: Microsoft 2000. Swift: Apple 2014.

OOP pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism. C is procedural and not OOP.
